# Layout


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

An itemized treemap shows how a set splits into subsets, and subsets
into sub-subsets, with every member written out. Each item is one cell
of a grid; each group, at every depth, is one connected region of cells;
and the whole map is a rectangle whose only carve-out is the end of its
last column.

## How the cells are placed

Cells are laid along a **snake**: down the first column, up the second,
down the third, and so on, through a grid `h` rows tall. Every group
gets one unbroken run of that path, so every group’s region is
connected, at every depth, whatever the sizes.

Each group spends one to three cells on its **header** (its name). The
header goes where it reads best, tried in a fixed order:

1.  a whole row at the top or bottom edge of the region, so the header
    has no names beside it (*wide*: one line across cells; *tall*: the
    label broken down one column, one line per cell);
2.  otherwise the region’s top-left cell (or, when the region starts
    with a stub at the foot of a column, the top of the column holding
    most of it);
3.  otherwise the first cells of the region’s run.

Moving a header can leave a subgroup’s run touching its neighbour only
at a corner, so every choice is checked and the search backs up when
needed. The last option always works, because the remaining runs are
then still pieces of the snake.

Names inside a group are filled column by column, top to bottom, in
natural order, so the reading order does not depend on which way the
snake runs.

The layout depends only on integers: item counts and each header’s size
in cells (`Group.header_span`). Measuring text to choose those sizes
happens in [`treemap.render.prepare`](render.html).

### Item

``` python
def Item(
    name:str, value:float | None=None, numeral:str | None=None
)->None:
```

*One member of the map: its name, and optionally a value and the numeral
to print before the name.*

[`build_tree`](https://adamcc.github.io/itemiset/treemap/layout.html#build_tree)
turns `(path, item)` records into a tree, where `path` names the item’s
group at each level, e.g. `("Asia", "Eastern Asia")`. Subgroups smaller
than `min_group` are pooled into one “other” subgroup, and a group left
with a single subgroup absorbs it. Siblings are ordered largest first
(ties in natural order); groups named in `last` go at the end, in that
order.

### build_tree

``` python
def build_tree(
    records, min_group:int=1, other_label:str='other', order:str='size', last:tuple=(), labels:dict | None=None
)->__main__.Group:
```

*A
[`Group`](https://adamcc.github.io/itemiset/treemap/layout.html#group)
tree from `(path, Item)` records. `labels` maps group names to shorter
header text.*

``` python
recs = [(("Fruit", "Citrus"), Item(n)) for n in ["lime", "lemon", "orange"]] + \
       [(("Fruit", "Berry"), Item(n)) for n in ["fig"]] + \
       [(("Vegetable", "Root"), Item(n)) for n in ["carrot", "beet"]]
t = build_tree(recs, min_group=2)
test_eq([c.name for c in t.children], ["Fruit", "Vegetable"])
test_eq([c.label or c.name for c in t.children[0].children], ["Citrus", "other"])   # Berry (1 item) pooled
test_eq([it.name for it in t.children[1].items], ["beet", "carrot"])               # lone subgroup merged
test_eq(t.n_items(), 6)
test_eq(t.n_cells(root=True), 6 + 2 + 2)   # items + top-level headers + Fruit's two subgroup headers
test_fail(lambda: build_tree([(("A",), Item("x")), (("A", "B"), Item("y"))]), contains="both items and subgroups")
```

``` python
    h:int, n:int

```

*The first `n` cells of a path down column 0, up column 1, down column
2, … in a grid `h` rows tall.*

``` python
test_eq(snake(3, 7), [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (1, 1), (1, 0), (2, 0)])
assert connected(snake(3, 7)[2:6])          # any run of the snake is one piece
assert not connected([(0, 0), (1, 1)])      # corners do not count
```

``` python
    kind:str, path:tuple, item:__main__.Item | None=None, group:__main__.Group | None=None, span:tuple=()
)->None:
```

*What sits in a cell: an item, or part of a group’s header.*

The grid’s height is chosen to bring the map’s shape close to
`target_aspect` (width over height), given each cell’s shape
(`cell_aspect`), while avoiding a nearly empty last column. Every height
from 1 up is scored, the score is rounded to an integer, and the first
lowest wins.

### check_layout

``` python
def check_layout(
    lay:__main__.Layout
)->dict:
```

*The layout’s guarantees, each `True` or `False`.*

A small map, drawn as text: `#` marks header cells, letters the items.

``` python
def text_grid(lay):
    rows = [["." for _ in range(lay.cols)] for _ in range(lay.h)]
    for (c, r), p in lay.cells.items():
        rows[r][c] = "#" if p.kind == "header" else p.item.name[0]
    return "\n".join("".join(r) for r in rows)

lay = layout_tree(t, cell_aspect=3, h=4)
print(lay)
print(text_grid(lay))
assert all(check_layout(lay).values())
```

A header can span cells. Here Fruit’s header takes two cells side by
side, and the map grows by one cell:

``` python
t.children[0].header_span = 2
lay2 = layout_tree(t, cell_aspect=3, h=4)
print(text_grid(lay2))
assert all(check_layout(lay2).values())
t.children[0].header_span = 1
```

## Randomised check

Random trees one to three levels deep, with random header sizes, laid
out at every height: every layout must keep all its guarantees.

``` python
def random_tree(rng, depth, prefix="g"):
    g = Group(prefix)
    g.header_span = rng.choice((1, 1, 2, 3))
    g.header_lines = ["x"] * g.header_span if rng.random() < 0.6 else None
    if depth == 0:
        g.items = [Item(f"{prefix}i{k}") for k in range(rng.randint(1, 12))]
    else:
        g.children = [random_tree(rng, depth - 1, f"{prefix}.{k}") for k in range(rng.randint(1, 6))]
    return g

n_layouts = 0
for seed in range(60):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    root = Group("root", children=[random_tree(rng, rng.randint(0, 2), f"t{k}") for k in range(rng.randint(1, 8))])
    for h in range(2, min(root.n_cells(root=True), 40) + 1):
        res = check_layout(layout_tree(root, cell_aspect=3, h=h))
        assert all(res.values()), (seed, h, res)
        n_layouts += 1
print(n_layouts, "random layouts, all valid")
```

    2160 random layouts, all valid
